en: May the Moon, the lord of Rohiṇī, who is adorned as a crest upon the head of Hara and whose rivalry with Him was once rivaled by the curved beauty of the creeper-like eyebrows of the Daughter of the Mountain, bring you prosperity— this work composed by the great poet Śrī Śambhu.
Pressing his breast against the lines of the marks made by the tips of the Goddess’s breasts and nails at the conclusion of their union, the moon-crested Lord bestows a flow of nectar.
May she protect you— she by whom the crescent moon of Hari’s head, through the play of his *tāṇḍava* dance,
has been dissolved into her crown, and which now serves as a camphor leaf-design upon the slope of her left breast.
O bees, purchase the measure of nectar by bartering away jasmine buds as ear-ornaments,
and leave your taste for pearl earrings; instead, apply it to the ears of Śambhu’s words,
which are as sweet as the *kreṅkāra* sound from the bow-stalk of Rati’s beloved.
Let not the mind be filled with longing, even when [the sound] is uttered from the cavity of the throat of the sweet-voiced cuckoo. || 3 ||
O Lord, when your fame— pervading the expanse of the sky, white as the moon, washing away the circle of the quarters, profoundly tranquil, and beloved by the world— is fully matured,
the mountains act like Kailāsa, the serpents act like Śeṣa, and the oceans act like the great sea.
The celestial elephants act like the Milky Ocean, and the male cuckoos act like swans.
On the slopes of the Kailāsa mountain, your glories were thus sung by the wives of the gods in voices as melodious as the warbling of the cuckoo;
even though you possess the playful grace of an ornament, you are like a jewel-lamp in the midst of love-making.
The sprout of the crescent moon upon his crest was immediately granted by the Conqueror of Cities as a mark of favor.
Stealing the crest-ornaments from the hair-tufts of the Cauḍīs, scattering the ear-pendants of the Karṇāṭīs,
robbing the flute of the Keralīs and their play with necklaces, and making the foreheads of the Lāṭīs— those very ornaments of the earth— devoid of their tilaka-mark, he [advanced].
May your unique sword, the whetstone for the gold of your ever-new fame, be victorious!
For the pacification of the arrogant, for the victory of the worlds, for the prosperity of those who ask, for the honor of the virtuous, for the welfare of the great, and for the distress of kings—
you were created by the Creator with joy, curiosity, with meditation stilled, with Vedic recitation set aside, and with all ascetic toil brought to an end.
O Indra of the Earth, what else need be said? Before your prowess, even the three-strided stride of Viṣṇu, though its movement was unimpeded in the sky, can no longer claim preeminence anywhere.
O King, listen! In the city of the gods, in the world of men, and in the realm of the serpents, there have been some [rulers], there are some now, and there will be some in the future;

yet among them, there has never been, is not, nor will there ever be anyone equal to you in statesmanship, in humility, in beauty, in devotion to poetry, in wisdom, or in the destruction of enemies and the spread of fame.
"O Ānandā, Mucukundā, Kandali, embrace me; you are well, O Vāsantika!
May it be well with you, O Mallikā; you have become healthy, O Mālatī!
Since this fame has today reached the ears of all, it does not cause you [any distress]."
It resembles the breaking off of a fresh, juicy bud used as an ear-ornament by the fawn-eyed woman.
Do not remember Caitra; forget him! Remember Rati instead—why, O simple one, do you vainly bind your leather thong with murderous arrows? Cast away your bow, firm though it be in its stringing!
For when this God is remembered even once, there remains for fair-browed women neither thought, nor memory, nor stability, nor attachment, nor fortitude, nor even any peace anywhere.
The city of Gauḍa abandons its golden bracelets as they slip off;
Kauṅkaṇa enters the forest, overwhelmed and with his hair disheveled;
and Kauntala [flees], while you, O Lion, roar a terrifying sound in your rising wrath—what more need be said?
The Mālava, having fallen from his lineage, enters the realm of Māra. || 12 ||
Having heard that story of your beauty— flowing like nectar into the ears of celestial damsels— recited by joyful bards in the palace of Indra,
he casts aside his bow, abandons his arrow, and, though he feels sorrow, finds no delight.
The God of Love, his intense agony gradually subsiding, looks with indifference upon the variegated month of Caitra.

That splendor which exists in the strings of pearls on head-dresses, in the flower-garlands in the braided hair of Kerala women, in the ivory pavilions of the Colas, and in the playful smiles of Muralī—
alas, even as it reaches the farthest limit of eclipsing the rays of the moon, today’s great poets both perceive this dark luster and censure it in the presence of your glories.

The beautiful women among your enemies have become like rivers: their passion has ebbed away due to the arrows of the God of Love, they are agitated by swarms of restless waves, they are dull-witted, and they have made their dwellings in the darkness. 15.
Bearing a dark spot upon his lap—the mass of hair of the beautiful Kerala women—the foolish friend of the night (the moon) falsely ascends the peak of the eastern mountain;
for your glories, possessing the luster of the leaves of the *tāpiccha* tree, dispel that darkness and smear the treasury of the world as if with camphor and liquid mercury. 16.
When King Muñja had departed for heaven, she stood with the slopes of her breasts rippling with tremors, her lower lip washed by tears, and her hands pressed against her cheeks overcome by grief;
but now that you have arisen, she stands with her lovely necklace and bracelets tinkling, and her bangles jingling.
The Blessed Goddess of Speech dances, her golden girdle shimmering.
In solitude, she drew a portrait for a long time with a line full of elegance;
possessed of many fancies, she formed numerous mental constructions and even performed severe vows, following the opinion of another Prajāpati.
How much effort did the Creator not exert himself in the process of fashioning you? || 18 ||

O elephants of the quarters, cast off all remaining afflictions without exception; perform your own duties as you please, and sport at will in the creeper-thickets on the sandy banks of the ocean. May you traverse this entire earth, along with its mountains, cities, oceans, and rivers.
For the arm of the illustrious King Harṣa supports the earth together with its six continents.
O Heramba, desist from the clapping of your ears; O Cūḍāpagā, do not roar;
O humped one, do not, do not, do not make the jingling sound of golden bells around your neck, while the songs of your fame are being commenced by the gods before the Enemy of the Cities.
"Of one who is distracted"—these words of the joyful Nandin flash forth. 20.
Free from bracelets, waistbands, necklaces, and armlets, the fair-browed wives of the enemies of the desert-dwellers move with clever steps;
for the king holds in his hand a sword-blade that acts with pride.
This [arm] is the right one for those who are adversaries of the arm. || 21 ||
O Lord of Caṇḍī, place for a long time the sprout-like crescent moon upon the crest of your head; O ancient tortoise, go to the furthermost depths of the ocean;
O Brahmā, abandon your meditation and sprinkle the lotus-throne with water.
By which, O Lord, this mature fire of your majesty spreads forth on all sides. || 22 ||
Let there be disregard for Kandarpa, Nalakūbara,
and even the Moon; out of curiosity for those stories of your beauty that have been circulated by the gods,
Urvaśī has become emaciated, Rati is utterly exhausted, and Rohiṇī is ruined.
Moreover, Rambhā’s body was born with the onset of the intense fever of longing for her own husband.
Though full of delight, though full of effort, and though filled with intense longing, the fawn-eyed women do not reach the side of their lovers even within the darkness of the night;
for today, by your fame— which possesses a luster that surpasses the hue of a severed elephant tusk— they have been instantly [overwhelmed].
The darkness, as dark as the mass of hair of beautiful city women, has reached its cessation.
Nowhere did the path of the submarine fire, born from the churning of the ocean, ever reach exhaustion; yet, when that very ocean is being dried up by the fire of your majesty,
I suspect it falls into the mud and strives for the roots of young moss.
The Tortoise of Vaikuṇṭha performs some inscrutable action, restless upon the shore. || 25 ||
He observes his own mention in [great] compositions, learns supreme proficiency in speech, composes masterful arrangements of words, cultivates familiarity with the path of suggestion (dhvani),
and displays ingenuity in the art of expression in the presence of Bṛhaspati himself.
O Lord, what indeed does the Goddess of Speech not do in order to describe your virtues?
O Lord of Stars, whose dark spot is stilled and who are the ornament upon the crest of Śaṅkara,
wander now with playful grace and ever without fear in the lap of heaven;
for today, by his fame alone, you have been made visible throughout all seven worlds.
"You shall become Svarbhānu; you are no longer within the range of vision when your form is severed in the sky. || 27 ||
Now that you, a man of virtue, have been born, that Rāma—who was once the delight of the virtuous—is despondent when you are intent on renunciation; and that Karṇa has grown pale.
What more need we say? O destroyer of the city of the earth in battle, for one such as you, who is a master of the science of archery, that Pārtha would surely be rendered useless before you.
"O friend Śrītāmraparṇī, jewel of the ocean, create luster and diminish your exhaustion; for even the slightest blemish does not exist in you, the pearl-oyster.
Having beheld her fame—which steals away the exquisite beauty of the deer-bannered god [Kāma]—"
For the fawn-eyed women are indeed longing for a garland of liberated pearls. || 29 ||
Sleep does not visit the Lord of Wealth; that Lord of Laṅkā harbors constant apprehension in the sky; and he assumes the very form of the Sun, the lover of the lotus.
What more need be said, O Lord? If even the sprout of your creeper-like eyebrow quivers, Indra himself cries out, his hand pressed against his hollowed cheek.
The glory of Yayāti has set, vanished through hundreds of reports concerning Duṣyanta;

the fame of Śantanu has been stilled, and the renown of Raghu has become insignificant in the worlds. And what more need be said? Now that you, the full moon, have risen for the night-lotus of the earth—
Alas, O Lord, even such talk regarding Rāma has come to an end since his birth! (31)
May Girijā dance with her festive joy, her hair-locks swaying like a vine of playful pearls, her girdle-string tinkling, and her golden bracelets shimmering—
she who resounds with the clamor of dancing waves as she turns her face toward hearing of your fame.
The Mandākinī [was released] from the crown by him who wears the crescent of the moon as his crest-ornament.
Alas, O Lord, even during the day, the interior of the quarters has become as if flooded with camphor, mercury, and streams of nectar by your glories!
Having donned armor upon your body, having fastened your quiver, and having placed Mādhava before you—
Love, with the thought that the friend of the night-lotus has risen, runs forward, shaking his bow.

This sword of yours, Kṛṣṇa, shines forth— having brought the battle with Kaṃsa to its conclusion, renowned throughout the worlds, eager for the people of Gopana, and ever achieving victory over the Dānavas.
O old monkey marked by the crescent moon that adorns the head of the Destroyer of Rākā, at the hour of midnight while the celestial nymphs sing of your glory in a bower on Kailāsa,
drops of nectar were placed upon your eyes by Pārvatī to dispel the sleep born of exhaustion from the play of Love, after she had squeezed the moon-bud from the crown of her beloved’s head.
O Goddess of Speech, now that Muñja has departed, what is this exhaustion? What is this lack of peace? Or what is this instability?
Are you desolate? Are you agitated? Why are you so weary? What is this sequence of events?
Know him to be that very person himself; for he is his intellect, he is his renown, and he is his splendor.
That is true renunciation, that is true policy, that is the essence in eloquent sayings, and those are the riches esteemed by all.

O Mother, why do you delay? Have mercy! Dwell upon the tip of my tongue in whatever form you will; be present within my heart, O Goddess of Speech—salutations to you—whoever I am, a reckless man, as I respectfully describe the deeds of kings.
The mind remains with the expansion of love, the essence of curiosity, and joyful exuberance. || 37 ||
O Lord, as soon as your beautiful deeds were chanted by the clever celestial bards with voices that captivated the prideful cries of the enamored bees in the heavenly vault,
at that very moment, the lovely Smara— his rain of arrows already drawn— advanced before the celestial beauties whose tresses were bound with strings of pearls.

Your glories flow as streams of sandalwood paste upon the heart, pour forth as waves of nectar from the body, and stream with the essence of elixirs at the edge of the ear; they spread as a vanguard across the regions of the quarters, form a carpet of pearls upon the circle of the earth, and become moons in the lap of the sky. (39)
O Bull-bannered Lord, why fearlessly place the full moon upon the position of your crest today instead of that childish crescent moon which has the dull luster of a lotus fiber?
For by night, the fame of this God, possessing the brilliance of the inner petals of a ketaka flower, [surpasses it].
And in the limit of the sky, in the celestial sphere, and in all directions, darkness was scattered and gathered together.
It is not the month of Caitra with its clusters of mango buds that fashioned that bow; nor are these cruel, sharp-pointed arrows the cuckoos’ fifth-note song;
nor is it the moon with its unrestrained rays, nor the crocodile stationed upon the banner, nor even Rati herself. Yet, oh! You, O Manmatha, are the one who pierces the pride of all women.
I consider that embodied form to be nectar for a moment in this world; I know that very day to be the essence, and that night alone to be long with its virtues.
It is the abode of prosperity, the ground of fame, and the refuge even of the wise.
Wherever the fish-bannered god of love from Kashmir comes within the range of one's vision, [there he dwells].
O Mukunda, even though the end of the rainy season has arrived, do not, do not abandon the surface of your couch upon the serpent’s hood, embraced by the lovely arms of Lakṣmī;
for this [state] leads to the awakening of the steadfast and to the cessation of the wicked.
Girt for battle, he was the jewel that adorned the crowns of the virtuous, the Indra of the earth’s realm.
O Duṣyanta, praise has gone to your contempt, and lightness has gone to your [weight]; O Pārtha, the entire world falls into despondency, and your fame likewise falls into worthlessness,
now that this friend of the virtuous, this Dāmódhara (the moon) for the dark night of kings, has been born as the protector of the earth.
O Karṇa, your glories have not reached the ears of anyone here.
This earth, girt by the oceans, is well known; what indeed has not been considered therein?
Within that circle of Indra’s realm, even news of Maṇipur has reached us—news concerning beauty, fame, devotion, policy, familiarity, and the composition of poetry.
Until such time as there shall be no other person anywhere, at any time, who is your rival. || 45 ||
Thus do I entreat you, O Lotus-seated One: having ceased your curiosity for Vedic recitation, once again expand with effort the interior of the cosmic egg;
for the fame of this Lord—which is as pure as the interior of a blossoming white lotus opened by the playful rays of the full moon—is so vast that it cannot be contained within it.
Resting upon your arm, which bears the calluses of the bowstring and supports the entire earth, the Tortoise King has his fatigue entirely stilled; he performs some inscrutable act of sport,
holding a gathering to nibble the tender shoots of the *lavalī* creeper on the shore of the sea.
Then the elephants of the quarters drink simultaneously from the waters of the lord of rivers.

"O Menakā, why this silence? O Śacī, why do you bear such grief? O Dhṛtācī, what is this emaciation? O Rambhā, why is your lotus-face thus averted?"—such were the words spoken by their friends to the celestial damsels who were afflicted by the intense fever of love, once the nectar of your feet had reached the path of their ears, O Lord. (48)
Was it risen by the rays of the full moon? Was it emerged by pearls?
Was it smiled by jasmine buds? Was it blossomed by *mālatī* calyxes?
Was it grown by the playful laughter of beautiful women? Or was it scattered there by streams of nectar—in that place where your fame, O sole ornament of the three worlds, has wandered? (49)
The quarters of the sky are not unrestrained, nor is the expanse of the firmament thick with clouds; the surface of the netherworld is not agitated, nor is this earth again [disturbed].
Thus, O Lord, how indeed are your tusks, white as the severed tips of an elephant's tusk, [so radiant]?
And his glories, which pour forth streams of the nectar of sacred revelation, move at their own will and pervade all space. || 50 ||
He who was a fire to his enemies like Anila, a Nala, a lamp for the earth like Dilīpa;
he who was as broad as Pṛthu in pride, yet in the world Rāghava was free from vanity;
he who was devoted to fame like Bharata, and who, through royal virtues, was as tranquil as Śantanu.
O Lord of the Earth, once you were born, for whom were all those things not forgotten? (51)
On the shores of the boundless ocean, on the Himalayas, on the Mālaya mountain, on the exceedingly rugged and difficult-to-climb Rohaṇa,
and on Mount Mandara with its deep caverns, the celestial mountain sinks down.
Oh, your glories, having reached their full maturity, wander about but do not fall! 52.

The intention was conceived by Gaurī’s husband while seated upon his lotus-throne; the protection of the three worlds and the display of the prowess of your arms were achieved in the conquest of all the wondrous Dānavas.
Yet, O Lord, even in that, you felt no pride.
That which the god Brahmā, the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva), and the Beloved of Kamalā (Viṣṇu) performed in ancient times.
Magnanimity resides in the wealthy; policy in virtuous people; modesty in women of noble family; excellent poetry in the mouth; intoxication in the elephant; the male cuckoo in the forest;
the bee in the lotus; and the art of nail-marks upon the cheek of a beloved woman.
O Lord, you are the ornament upon the surface of the earth, while she is but a slender form upon the bed. 54.
Born within the heart of a lotus, the relic of the Blessed One has fulfilled its purpose; it is fitting that the Beloved of Ramā should soon establish his residence in the ocean.
O All-pervading Lord, as the fire of your mature majesty spreads everywhere, even that sprout of the crescent moon upon the head of the Wielder of the Pināka bow attains its fruitfulness.

O King, even on the desert sands, the sequence of amorous play remains consistent for the fair-browed wives of your enemies: a low moan from within their throats due to exhaustion from the sun’s rays; the contraction of the corners of their eyes from the swirling of dust; a hissing sound from wounds inflicted by the tips of sharp kuśa grass; and the rising waves of sighs born of fear of forest-dwellers. (56)
O Moon of the Earth, this is the message sent by the beloved of Śacī:

"O King, with palms joined in reverence, desist from your exertion toward the intensification of the fire of your mighty majesty; let these [arrows] instead become worthy ear-ornaments for the celestial nymphs."
The sprouts, having assumed the appearance of withered shoots upon the young shoots of the Nandana grove, have grown weary. || 57 ||

She possesses the power to burn away the intense heat of the mind; she reveals the hope for desire while shedding her self-restraint, yet she does not do so for the virtuous because of their universal abandonment of sin; she spreads forth mature and unceasing love, being both "the aged" and "the pure."
O Manobhava, though your fame is renowned throughout the earth, women are of diverse natures. || 58 ||
Whatever splendor there is in the moon that intoxicates, whatever depth there is in the ocean, whatever majesty resides in Mount Meru, whatever loftiness of power exists in the sun,
and whatever quality of valor even the Lord of Lakṣmī possesses— if you wish to see all of that gathered in one place, then behold this god, the jewel of the three worlds. (59)
He is renowned in the world as Trivikrama because of your many strides; by him alone was Bali slain—he who is the destroyer of hundreds of Balis and whose hand is your own.
Who does not know him as Vaikuṇṭha? You are indeed unimpeded in conquering the world. Thus, there is a great difference between you and that god who is the enemy of the Daityas.
Where Bhārgava received the blow from the pillar-like arm of Arjuna, powerful with intoxication;
where the Lord of the Raghus was the cutter of the forest that was the throat of the Ten-necked one;
and where even Pārtha defeated the Beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain in the guise of a Kirāta—whose arm-prowess there has not been celebrated by you with blossoming wonders? (51)
Alas, the female cakravāka birds, mistaking it for the rising of the moon, release a lotus sprout from their beaks and carry away their exhaustion there;
moreover, why does the male bird approach with his beak upturned, under the delusion that it is the light of the autumnal moon?
Alas, the row of cakora birds experiences pure joy where your stainless fame has arisen.
O Lord, the Kalpalatās drench themselves with many showers of frost; then the Santānakas apply incessant streams of water trickling from Śrīkhaṇḍa trees;
and even the Mandāra vines sufficiently moisten themselves with the thick liquid of moonstones.
Today, the women of heaven sprinkle [themselves with water] out of fear for the fire of your majesty.
The distress caused by the separation from Rāma has passed; the fever born of Duṣyanta’s restlessness has vanished; and all the sorrow arising from Nala’s absence has melted away.
Moreover, O Lord, while you bear this great imperial splendor—what more need be said?
Even Śāntanu’s son, though peaceful, was a certain vast separation from the earth.

O Lord, the water in the courtyard pond— fragrant from contact with blooming lotuses and remaining after the female elephants had drunk— was sipped at leisure by your enemies' wild elephants; they repeatedly scratched an itch on their temples against the *kurabaka* tree, its buds trembling with the jerks, while half-closing one eye-petal as if it were slightly budding.
Relax your fortitude, O Tortoise; abandon your steadfastness, O Śeṣa; and you, O Goddess Earth, do not harbor hope in those who make mere wishes their elephants.
This arm of this king, scarred by the bowstring, is capable of bearing even you, girdled by the moat of the seven oceans.

O Lord of the Earth, your glories—growing like young shoots upon the *ketaka* flowers—have wandered through wildernesses, forests, riverbanks, mountain laps, cities, and the shores of the ocean; now, as if weary, they take root in the lovely vicinity of the *nandana-kandalī* trees. (67)
"Is this the rising of the moon? Or is it the mountain, the father of Gaurī?
Is this the Ocean of Milk? Or is it the serpent of the playful sport of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva)?
Is this Mount Mandara, washed by the waves of the nectar-ocean?"
O Indra of the Earth, embodied beings are always filled with doubt regarding your fame.
I do not even recall a word of conversation with Nalakūbara, nor do I remember him;
what more need I say? I do not even pray for the sight of the moon, the bringer of nectar. Yet, if this [moon] should come within the range of my eyes, it would be a festival for my sight.
The protector of the earth was like the springtime for the honey-bees that were the minds of all his beloved women. || 69 ||
The *kunda* flower was released with budding anguish, the *vicakila* with trembling agitation, the *ketaka* with fear, the *madana* with dejection, and the *atimuktadruma* with lethargy; yet,
O Lord, they were unable to release you during your departure from the city.
At that time, Kesara, having performed his marriage to Mādhavī, was truly possessed of filaments (or: truly possessed of a beautiful wife). || 70 ||
O Pot-born Sage, is this not indeed consistent with the secret of your wisdom, that even the boundless Vindhya mountain— though it conceals both heaven and earth— has been rendered barren?
Otherwise, how could the fame of this Lord, which surpasses the rays of the autumnal moon, have pervaded the entire expanse of heaven and earth?
Fie upon that ear-ornament fashioned from a *mallī* flower;
let even that jeweled earring go to ruin and become useless!
O kings, you may only be made to serve as an ear-filler by the naturally simple and eloquent sayings of Śiva’s devotees. (72)
O slender one, although that low humming of yours— which flows like nectar to the ears and emerges from the throat-cavity of the sweet-voiced cuckoo— is uniquely the abode of softness,
nevertheless, it serves as an offering of life for the God of Beasts who was scorched by Śiva.
The fifth [note], which is favored by the five-arrowed god (Kāma), is enriched with aesthetic flavor and perfected through its maturation. || 73 ||
What need is there for necklaces, or bracelets, or flowers, or ear-ornaments?
Enough with armlets and jeweled earrings! Enough with ostentatious garments! In the opinion of Śambhu, this singular "mutilation" alone is the true ornament for men.
His well-spoken verses are like the flowing nectar from the crescent of the full moon when it is squeezed.

O Goddess of Speech, though your eloquence— which carries the essence of nectar for the wise and expands the beauty of the face of the brow— is ever devoted to serving you, it remains somehow ever-new;
yet, O Mother, there is this one prayer from Śambhu with palms joined in reverence.
May there be some person of sensitive mind, skilled in discerning the reality of things, who listens to my words. (75)
Thus ends the *Rājendrakarṇapūra*, composed by the great poet Śrī Śambhu, born in the land of Kaśmīra.
